title: PHASE: Physiology-Aware Hyperspectral Reconstruction via Object-to-Human Domain Adaptation

problem.claim: Bulky hardware, slow acquisition, and regulatory burden limit the clinical availability of hyperspectral imaging.

gap.claim: Existing object-centric reconstruction paradigms rely on reflectance-based feature alignment and fail when visually similar RGB responses correspond to distinct, entangled physiological states.

contributions.claim: PHASE is a physiology-aware hyperspectral reconstruction paradigm for object-to-human transfer.
PHASE disentangles cross-channel physiological semantics through Physiological Channel Reinterpretation.
PHASE restricts reconstruction to physiologically plausible solutions through Physiologically Constrained Alignment.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across two source-to-target transfer protocols, PHASE reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to +2.20 SSIM and -3.06 in SAM with 1.5% labeled supervision.

narrative_sequence.summary: Clinical availability of hyperspectral imaging is limited by hardware, acquisition, and regulatory constraints.
Hyperspectral information can be reconstructed from ubiquitous RGB or CASSI measurements.
Object-centric reflectance alignment fails for physiological imaging because RGB similarity does not reliably preserve physiological semantics.
PHASE addresses cross-channel semantic shifts and irreversible RGB information loss using physiology-aware semantic disentanglement and constrained alignment.
The authors report gains over state-of-the-art methods under two transfer protocols with limited labeled supervision.

source_observation.claim: Reflectance-based feature alignment can fail when visually similar measurements arise from different underlying physiological states.

interpretation.claim: Domain adaptation should align representations using domain-relevant semantics rather than relying only on visual or reflectance similarity.

application.claim: For physiological imaging, incorporate representations or constraints tied to shared light–matter interaction principles.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this lesson generalizes beyond physiological imaging or the stated transfer setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, or protocol details.
The abstract does not define the evaluation conditions or the meaning of the reported SAM change.
The abstract does not describe the extent or causes of irreversible information loss in RGB acquisition.
